claim: The domestication of maize began nine thousand years ago when Mexican farmers started to collect the seeds of the wild grass, teosinte.
source: The natural history of maize began nine thousand years ago when Mexican farmers started to collect the seeds of the wild grass, teosinte.
evidence: This is a temporal claim about the origin of maize domestication, presented as established fact in the abstract.

claim: Genetic data point to the tropical Balsas river valley in Mexico as the site where maize (Zea mays ssp. mays) was domesticated from teosinte (Zea mays ssp. parviglumis).
source: Genetic data point to the tropical Balsas river valley in Mexico as the site where maize (Zea mays ssp. mays) was domesticated from teosinte (Zea mays ssp. parviglumis) (Matsuoka et al., 2002; van Heerwaarden et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Matsuoka et al., 2002; van Heerwaarden et al., 2011).

claim: Archeological data support the Balsas river valley location for maize domestication.
source: Archeological data support this location and also suggest that squash may have been domesticated at the same time (Piperno et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Piperno et al., 2009.

claim: Squash may have been domesticated at the same time as maize.
source: Archeological data support this location and also suggest that squash may have been domesticated at the same time (Piperno et al., 2009).
evidence: This speculative claim is supported by citation to Piperno et al., 2009, with the word 'suggest' indicating uncertainty.

claim: Some think maize was first collected for the fermentable sugars in its stalk.
source: Some think maize was first collected for the fermentable sugars in its stalk (Iltis, 2000; Smalley and Blake, 2003), but more likely it was for the storable starch in its seed.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations to Iltis, 2000 and Smalley and Blake, 2003.

claim: Maize was more likely first collected for the storable starch in its seed rather than for fermentable sugars in its stalk.
source: Some think maize was first collected for the fermentable sugars in its stalk (Iltis, 2000; Smalley and Blake, 2003), but more likely it was for the storable starch in its seed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' assessment, indicated by 'more likely'.

claim: Teosinte disperses pollen in the wind.
source: In addition to dispersing pollen in the wind, the kernels fall from the plant and, if eaten, are carried to other locations in fecal matter, thanks to the indigestible fruitcase (see Box 1 for a glossary of specialist terms used in this article).
evidence: This is a statement about teosinte biology presented as established knowledge.

claim: Teosinte kernels fall from the plant and can be carried to other locations in fecal matter due to the indigestible fruitcase.
source: In addition to dispersing pollen in the wind, the kernels fall from the plant and, if eaten, are carried to other locations in fecal matter, thanks to the indigestible fruitcase (see Box 1 for a glossary of specialist terms used in this article).
evidence: This is a statement about teosinte seed dispersal mechanism presented as established knowledge.

claim: The domestication of maize kept the wind-born pollen of teosinte.
source: The domestication of maize kept the wind-born pollen of teosinte, but changed other traits, improving its utility for human consumption (Doebley, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Doebley, 2004.

claim: The domestication of maize changed traits other than pollen dispersal, improving its utility for human consumption.
source: The domestication of maize kept the wind-born pollen of teosinte, but changed other traits, improving its utility for human consumption (Doebley, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Doebley, 2004.

claim: The teosinte fruitcase became softer during domestication, allowing humans to grind its kernels for food.
source: The teosinte fruitcase, full of silica and lignin, became softer (Figure 1C), allowing humans to grind its kernels for food.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1C showing the difference between teosinte and maize kernels.

claim: The teosinte fruitcase is full of silica and lignin.
source: The teosinte fruitcase, full of silica and lignin, became softer (Figure 1C), allowing humans to grind its kernels for food.
evidence: This is a statement about the composition of the teosinte fruitcase presented as established knowledge.

claim: The branch holding the kernels (cob) grew in girth during domestication, increasing the kernel row number from 2 to 20, or more.
source: The branch holding the kernels (cob) grew in girth, increasing the kernel row number from 2 to 20, or more (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1D showing the comparison between teosinte and maize.

claim: Maize kernels no longer self-dispersed but were held tight on the cob, requiring the intervention of humans to sow seeds.
source: Kernels no longer self-dispersed but were held tight on the cob, requiring the intervention of humans to sow seeds.
evidence: This is a statement about a key domestication trait presented as established knowledge.

claim: During maize domestication, the long branches shortened but kept the leaves along the branch.
source: Finally, the long branches shortened, but kept the leaves along the branch.
evidence: This is a statement about morphological changes during domestication presented as established knowledge.

claim: The husk leaves keep birds, insects and other pests from eating the kernels.
source: These 'husk leaves' keep birds, insects and other pests from eating the kernels.
evidence: This is a functional claim about husk leaves presented as established knowledge.

claim: From the Balsas region of Mexico, maize spread north and south.
source: From the Balsas region of Mexico, maize spread north and south (Matsuoka et al., 2002), adapting to very different environmental conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Matsuoka et al., 2002.

claim: Maize adapted to very different environmental conditions as it spread from the Balsas region.
source: From the Balsas region of Mexico, maize spread north and south (Matsuoka et al., 2002), adapting to very different environmental conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the geographic spread of maize and citation to Matsuoka et al., 2002.

claim: Maize is now found growing across a wider area than any other major crop.
source: In a testament to its adaptability, maize is now found growing across a wider area than any other major crop (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 2 showing the geographic distribution of maize cultivation.

claim: Major morphological changes in maize had occurred by 6500 years ago.
source: Cobs of corn found in archeological sites suggest that major morphological changes had occurred by 6500 years ago (Piperno and Flannery, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Piperno and Flannery, 2001 and archeological evidence.

claim: Pollen flow between domesticated maize and other teosinte taxa contributed to some of its diversification.
source: Pollen flow between domesticated maize and other teosinte taxa contributed to some of its diversification (van Heerwaarden et al., 2011), and local adaptation and trade continue to shape maize genetic diversity (Mercer et al., 2008; Ruiz Corral et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to van Heerwaarden et al., 2011.

claim: Local adaptation and trade continue to shape maize genetic diversity.
source: Pollen flow between domesticated maize and other teosinte taxa contributed to some of its diversification (van Heerwaarden et al., 2011), and local adaptation and trade continue to shape maize genetic diversity (Mercer et al., 2008; Ruiz Corral et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mercer et al., 2008 and Ruiz Corral et al., 2008.

claim: Maize varieties in Mexico can often be distinguished by kernel or cob traits.
source: Maize varieties in Mexico can often be distinguished by kernel or cob traits (Vielle-Calzada and Padilla, 2009) but genetic diversity within these open-pollinated populations remains high (Pressoir and Berthaud, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vielle-Calzada and Padilla, 2009.

claim: Genetic diversity within open-pollinated maize populations in Mexico remains high.
source: Maize varieties in Mexico can often be distinguished by kernel or cob traits (Vielle-Calzada and Padilla, 2009) but genetic diversity within these open-pollinated populations remains high (Pressoir and Berthaud, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pressoir and Berthaud, 2004.

claim: Darwin was the first to recognize inbreeding depression in maize.
source: Darwin was the first to recognize inbreeding depression (see Glossary) in maize, a critical component of maize breeding.
evidence: This is a historical claim presented as established knowledge.

claim: Inbreeding depression is a critical component of maize breeding.
source: Darwin was the first to recognize inbreeding depression (see Glossary) in maize, a critical component of maize breeding.
evidence: This is an assessment of the importance of inbreeding depression in maize breeding.

claim: Darwin noted a reduced size in self-pollinated corn and the improved size and vigor, or heterosis, of cross-pollinated corn.
source: He noted a reduced size in self-pollinated corn and the improved size and vigor, or heterosis, of cross-pollinated corn (Darwin, 1876).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Darwin, 1876.

claim: George Harrison Shull made inbreds by self-pollinating maize plants for multiple generations before crossing them together to make hybrids.
source: His observations were extended by George Harrison Shull in 1908, who made inbreds by self-pollinating maize plants for multiple generations before crossing them together to make hybrids (Shull, 1908).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shull, 1908.

claim: Hybrid maize is the predominant form grown in industrial agriculture today.
source: Today, of course, hybrid maize is the predominant form grown in industrial agriculture (Duvick, 2001), with traditional open-pollinated landraces (see Glossary) primarily limited to small scale or subsistence farming.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Duvick, 2001.

claim: Traditional open-pollinated landraces are primarily limited to small scale or subsistence farming.
source: Today, of course, hybrid maize is the predominant form grown in industrial agriculture (Duvick, 2001), with traditional open-pollinated landraces (see Glossary) primarily limited to small scale or subsistence farming.
evidence: This is a statement about current agricultural practices presented as established knowledge.

claim: Teosinte is sensitive to day length and only makes flowers when days are short.
source: Teosinte is sensitive to day length and only makes flowers when days are short (Emerson, 1924).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Emerson, 1924.

claim: An important step in breeding maize for higher latitudes involved overriding environmental control of flowering, creating maize plants that flower independently of day length.
source: An important step in breeding maize for higher latitudes involved overriding this environmental control, creating maize plants that flower independently of day length.
evidence: This is a statement about maize breeding history presented as established knowledge.

claim: The maize shoot apical meristem initiates a genetically determined number of leaves before it transitions to become the male reproductive structure, known as the tassel.
source: The maize shoot apical meristem (see Glossary) initiates a genetically determined number of leaves before it transitions to become the male reproductive structure, known as the tassel.
evidence: This is a statement about maize developmental biology presented as established knowledge.

claim: Buds are found in the axils of most leaves in maize.
source: Buds are found in the axils (see Glossary) of most leaves—the lower buds become tillers, which are long branches, resembling the main stem.
evidence: This is a statement about maize morphology presented as established knowledge.

claim: The lower buds in maize become tillers, which are long branches resembling the main stem.
source: Buds are found in the axils (see Glossary) of most leaves—the lower buds become tillers, which are long branches, resembling the main stem.
evidence: This is a statement about maize developmental biology presented as established knowledge.

claim: The buds above the tillers will develop into the ears, which hold the kernels.
source: The buds above the tillers will develop into the ears, which hold the kernels.
evidence: This is a statement about maize developmental biology presented as established knowledge.

claim: During early development, the ear and tassel primordia appear similar to each other.
source: During early development, the ear and tassel primordia appear similar to each other (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 3A and 3B showing scanning electron microscopy images of tassel and ear primordia.

claim: Sex determination genes initiate a program that blocks development of female reproductive parts in the male flowers of the tassel and male reproductive parts in the female flowers of the ear.
source: Sex determination genes initiate a program that blocks development of female reproductive parts in the male flowers of the tassel and male reproductive parts in the female flowers of the ear (Cheng et al., 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cheng et al., 1983.

claim: The tassel of a tiller is often partially feminized.
source: Interestingly, the tassel of a tiller is often partially feminized.
evidence: This is an observation about maize biology presented as established knowledge.

claim: Teosinte plants have multiple tillers, ensuring a supply of pollen over many days.
source: While teosinte plants have multiple tillers, ensuring a supply of pollen over many days, modern maize often has a single tassel and lacks tillers entirely.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about teosinte and maize morphology presented as established knowledge.

claim: Modern maize often has a single tassel and lacks tillers entirely.
source: While teosinte plants have multiple tillers, ensuring a supply of pollen over many days, modern maize often has a single tassel and lacks tillers entirely.
evidence: This is a statement about modern maize morphology presented as established knowledge.

claim: Maize hybrids are created by planting two distinct inbreds in alternate rows and detasseling one inbred, ensuring that the ears on detasseled plants are cross-pollinated and thus hybrid.
source: Maize hybrids are created by planting two distinct inbreds in alternate rows and detasseling one inbred, ensuring that the ears on detasseled plants are cross-pollinated and thus hybrid.
evidence: This is a description of hybrid maize production methods presented as established knowledge.

claim: The male sperm in maize is carried in the pollen.
source: As with other flowering plants, the male sperm is carried in the pollen.
evidence: This is a statement about plant reproductive biology presented as established knowledge.

claim: Following meiosis, the microspore undergoes two mitotic divisions, generating two sperm cells contained within a vegetative cell.
source: Following meiosis, the microspore undergoes two mitotic divisions, generating two sperm cells contained within a vegetative cell (see Glossary).
evidence: This is a statement about maize reproductive biology presented as established knowledge.

claim: The vegetative nucleus does the work of bringing the sperm cells to the female egg.
source: The vegetative nucleus does the work of bringing the sperm cells to the female egg.
evidence: This is a statement about plant reproductive biology presented as established knowledge.

claim: The pollen germinates on silks, the extended pistils of the female flower, and grows a tube inside the silk.
source: The pollen germinates on silks, the extended pistils (see Glossary) of the female flower, and grows a tube inside the silk.
evidence: This is a statement about maize reproductive biology presented as established knowledge.

claim: Once the pollen tube reaches the plant's ovule, one sperm will fertilize the haploid egg cell, creating the diploid embryo.
source: Once the pollen tube reaches the plant's ovule, one sperm will fertilize the haploid egg cell, creating the diploid embryo, and the other sperm will fertilize the central cell of the female gametophyte, which has two polar nuclei (see Glossary).
evidence: This is a statement about double fertilization in maize presented as established knowledge.

claim: The other sperm will fertilize the central cell of the female gametophyte, which has two polar nuclei.
source: Once the pollen tube reaches the plant's ovule, one sperm will fertilize the haploid egg cell, creating the diploid embryo, and the other sperm will fertilize the central cell of the female gametophyte, which has two polar nuclei (see Glossary).
evidence: This is a statement about double fertilization in maize presented as established knowledge.

claim: The resulting triploid cell develops into the endosperm, a sacrificial tissue that feeds the growing embryo.
source: The resulting triploid cell develops into the endosperm, a sacrificial tissue that feeds the growing embryo.
evidence: This is a statement about maize seed development presented as established knowledge.

claim: The maize kernel can be stored for years in a dry state once it matures.
source: Once the kernel, containing the double fertilization event, matures, it can be planted or stored for years in a dry state.
evidence: This is a statement about maize seed storage properties presented as established knowledge.

claim: The root emerges first from the germinating maize kernel, growing towards gravity.
source: The root emerges first, growing towards gravity.
evidence: This is a statement about maize germination presented as established knowledge.

claim: The shoot grows upward, supported by the nutrients of the endosperm.
source: The shoot grows upward, supported by the nutrients of the endosperm (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 3C showing a germinated maize seedling.

claim: Maize is a monocotyledonous plant, meaning it produces one embryonic leaf.
source: Maize is a monocotyledonous plant, meaning it produces one embryonic leaf (as compared to another model plant Arabidopsis thaliana, which is a dicotyledonous plant).
evidence: This is a statement about plant classification presented as established knowledge.

claim: Arabidopsis thaliana is a dicotyledonous plant.
source: Maize is a monocotyledonous plant, meaning it produces one embryonic leaf (as compared to another model plant Arabidopsis thaliana, which is a dicotyledonous plant).
evidence: This is a statement about plant classification presented as established knowledge.

claim: The cotyledon equivalent for maize is the coleoptile, which is connected to the nutritive scutellum.
source: The cotyledon equivalent for maize is the coleoptile, which is connected to the nutritive scutellum (see Glossary).
evidence: This is a statement about maize anatomy presented as established knowledge.

claim: Inside the tubular coleoptile are sequentially younger leaves that arise from a shoot apical meristem.
source: Inside the tubular coleoptile are sequentially younger leaves that arise from a shoot apical meristem.
evidence: This is a statement about maize developmental anatomy presented as established knowledge.

claim: Geneticists began collecting, describing and distributing maize mutants in the early 1900's.
source: Geneticists began collecting, describing and distributing maize mutants in the early 1900's (see references in Emerson et al., 1935).
evidence: This historical claim is supported by citation to Emerson et al., 1935.

claim: Dozens of genes affect the texture of the endosperm and the color of its outermost layer, the aleurone.
source: Dozens of genes affect the texture of the endosperm and the color of its outermost layer, the aleurone, providing easily visible and eye-catching information about the genotype of the next generation.
evidence: This is a statement about maize genetics presented as established knowledge.

claim: Genes affecting endosperm texture and aleurone color provide easily visible and eye-catching information about the genotype of the next generation.
source: Dozens of genes affect the texture of the endosperm and the color of its outermost layer, the aleurone, providing easily visible and eye-catching information about the genotype of the next generation.
evidence: This is an inference about the utility of these genetic markers.

claim: The large, distinctive chromosomes of maize paved the way for a number of major discoveries, including linking genetic recombination to physical exchange of chromosomal segments.
source: The large, distinctive chromosomes of maize further paved the way for a number of major discoveries, including linking genetic recombination to physical exchange of chromosomal segments (Creighton and McClintock, 1931).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Creighton and McClintock, 1931.

claim: The copious amounts of pollen maize plants produce can be easily gathered and mutagenized with chemicals to create new mutant plants.
source: The copious amounts of pollen maize plants produce can be easily gathered and mutagenized with chemicals to create new mutant plants, allowing researchers to easily screen for even lethal mutations (Neuffer, 1993; Candela and Hake, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Neuffer, 1993 and Candela and Hake, 2008.

claim: Mutagenized pollen allows researchers to easily screen for even lethal mutations.
source: The copious amounts of pollen maize plants produce can be easily gathered and mutagenized with chemicals to create new mutant plants, allowing researchers to easily screen for even lethal mutations (Neuffer, 1993; Candela and Hake, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Neuffer, 1993 and Candela and Hake, 2008.

claim: Transposable elements were first described by Barbara McClintock.
source: Transposable elements (see Glossary), first described by Barbara McClintock (McClintock, 1950), continue to be an important tool for cloning genes based on mutant phenotype, and their use has provided novel insights into epigenetics (Lisch, 2012), such as the relationship between transposon activity and DNA methylation (Chandler and Walbot, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McClintock, 1950.

claim: Transposable elements continue to be an important tool for cloning genes based on mutant phenotype.
source: Transposable elements (see Glossary), first described by Barbara McClintock (McClintock, 1950), continue to be an important tool for cloning genes based on mutant phenotype, and their use has provided novel insights into epigenetics (Lisch, 2012), such as the relationship between transposon activity and DNA methylation (Chandler and Walbot, 1986).
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of transposable elements presented as established knowledge.

claim: The use of transposable elements has provided novel insights into epigenetics.
source: Transposable elements (see Glossary), first described by Barbara McClintock (McClintock, 1950), continue to be an important tool for cloning genes based on mutant phenotype, and their use has provided novel insights into epigenetics (Lisch, 2012), such as the relationship between transposon activity and DNA methylation (Chandler and Walbot, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lisch, 2012.

claim: Transposable elements have provided insights into the relationship between transposon activity and DNA methylation.
source: Transposable elements (see Glossary), first described by Barbara McClintock (McClintock, 1950), continue to be an important tool for cloning genes based on mutant phenotype, and their use has provided novel insights into epigenetics (Lisch, 2012), such as the relationship between transposon activity and DNA methylation (Chandler and Walbot, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chandler and Walbot, 1986.

claim: Maize and teosinte are members of the grass family Poaceae, which includes more than 10,000 species.
source: Maize and teosinte are members of the grass family Poaceae, which includes more than 10,000 species (Kellogg, 1998), including the major cereals, such as wheat and rice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kellogg, 1998.

claim: The grass family Poaceae includes the major cereals, such as wheat and rice.
source: Maize and teosinte are members of the grass family Poaceae, which includes more than 10,000 species (Kellogg, 1998), including the major cereals, such as wheat and rice.
evidence: This is a statement about plant taxonomy presented as established knowledge.

claim: The subfamily that includes Zea is Panicoideae (3236 species).
source: The subfamily that includes Zea is Panicoideae (3236 species), which also includes C4 energy crops (see Glossary) such as switchgrass, sorghum, miscanthus and the recently sequenced model, Setaria (Grass Phylogeny Working Group II, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Grass Phylogeny Working Group II, 2012.

claim: Panicoideae includes C4 energy crops such as switchgrass, sorghum, miscanthus and the recently sequenced model, Setaria.
source: The subfamily that includes Zea is Panicoideae (3236 species), which also includes C4 energy crops (see Glossary) such as switchgrass, sorghum, miscanthus and the recently sequenced model, Setaria (Grass Phylogeny Working Group II, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Grass Phylogeny Working Group II, 2012.

claim: Wheat, barley, and the model Brachypodium are in the Pooideae subfamily (3850 species).
source: Wheat, barley, and the model Brachypodium are in the Pooideae subfamily (3850 species), while rice, a well-studied model, as well as an important crop, is in the Ehrartoideae (111 species) (Grass Phylogeny Working Group II, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Grass Phylogeny Working Group II, 2012.

claim: Rice is in the Ehrartoideae (111 species).
source: Wheat, barley, and the model Brachypodium are in the Pooideae subfamily (3850 species), while rice, a well-studied model, as well as an important crop, is in the Ehrartoideae (111 species) (Grass Phylogeny Working Group II, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Grass Phylogeny Working Group II, 2012.

claim: The Pooideae and Ehrartoideae subfamilies contain only C3 grasses.
source: The latter two subfamilies contain only C3 grasses.
evidence: This is a statement about grass photosynthetic pathways presented as established knowledge.

claim: Despite the difference of more than 60 million years of evolution, studies of grass genomes have revealed that significant portions of their chromosomes share the same gene arrangement.
source: Despite the difference of more than 60 million years of evolution, studies of grass genomes have revealed that significant portions of their chromosomes share the same gene arrangement (Moore et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Moore et al., 1995.

claim: The discovery of shared gene arrangement provides an opportunity to isolate genes based on common positions of shared markers.
source: This discovery provides an opportunity to isolate genes based on common positions of shared markers.
evidence: This is an inference about the utility of synteny for gene identification.

claim: Researchers can take advantage of comparative genomics to identify orthologous genes and regulatory elements that are likely to be important for biological processes.
source: With the ever-increasing number of sequenced grass genomes, such as rice, sorghum, Brachypodium, Setaria and maize (https://genomevolution.org/wiki/index.php/Sequenced_plant_genomes#Grasses), researchers can now take advantage of comparative genomics to identify orthologous genes and regulatory elements that are likely to be important for biological processes (Lin et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lin et al., 2012.

claim: George Beadle was the first to cross maize with teosinte and examine the F2 progeny.
source: George Beadle was the first to cross maize with teosinte and examine the F2 progeny (Beadle 1972).
evidence: This historical claim is supported by citation to Beadle 1972.

claim: Based on the frequency of maize- or teosinte-like plants in his cross, Beadle argued that as few as five loci might be responsible for much of the phenotypic difference between maize and teosinte.
source: Based on the frequency of maize- or teosinte-like plants in his cross, he argued that as few as five loci might be responsible for much of the phenotypic difference between maize and teosinte.
evidence: This is a historical claim about Beadle's inference from his experimental data.

claim: Later work by John Doebley et al. found quantitative trait loci (QTL) consistent with Beadle's idea.
source: Later work by John Doebley et al. found quantitative trait loci (QTL; see Glossary) consistent with this idea (Doebley and Stec, 1991, 1993), and careful genetic analysis of these regions allowed Doebley's group to dissect some of these QTL down to the responsible genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Doebley and Stec, 1991, 1993.

claim: Careful genetic analysis of QTL regions allowed Doebley's group to dissect some of these QTL down to the responsible genes.
source: Later work by John Doebley et al. found quantitative trait loci (QTL; see Glossary) consistent with this idea (Doebley and Stec, 1991, 1993), and careful genetic analysis of these regions allowed Doebley's group to dissect some of these QTL down to the responsible genes.
evidence: This is a statement about the results of genetic analysis presented as established knowledge.

claim: tb1 is responsible for the shortening and feminization of the axillary branches in domesticated maize.
source: tb1 is responsible for the shortening and feminization of the axillary branches in domesticated maize (Doebley et al., 1997; Studer et al., 2011), while tga is responsible for the hardened fruitcase of teosinte (Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Doebley et al., 1997 and Studer et al., 2011.

claim: tga is responsible for the hardened fruitcase of teosinte.
source: tb1 is responsible for the shortening and feminization of the axillary branches in domesticated maize (Doebley et al., 1997; Studer et al., 2011), while tga is responsible for the hardened fruitcase of teosinte (Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2005.

claim: Changes at tb1 are due to genetic alterations at distant regulatory sequences.
source: Changes at tb1 are due to genetic alterations at distant regulatory sequences while critical changes at tga are likely to be due to amino-acid changes.
evidence: This is a statement about the molecular basis of tb1 changes presented as established knowledge.

claim: Critical changes at tga are likely to be due to amino-acid changes.
source: Changes at tb1 are due to genetic alterations at distant regulatory sequences while critical changes at tga are likely to be due to amino-acid changes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement indicated by 'likely to be'.

claim: Knowledge of tb1 and tga loci provides some of the best examples to date of how human selection for certain physical traits in maize has led to specific changes at the DNA level.
source: Knowledge of these loci provides some of the best examples to date of how human selection for certain physical traits in maize has led to specific changes at the DNA level.
evidence: This is an assessment of the significance of these findings.

claim: Many other genes, in addition to tb1 and tga1, have played a role in domestication.
source: Many other genes, in addition to tb1 and tga1, have played a role in domestication, however.
evidence: This is a statement about the genetic basis of domestication presented as established knowledge.

claim: The analysis of genetic diversity from whole-genome sequences of multiple maize and teosinte has identified nearly 500 regions of the genome that show evidence of selection during domestication.
source: The analysis of genetic diversity from whole-genome sequences of multiple maize and teosinte has identified nearly 500 regions of the genome that show evidence of selection during domestication (Hufford et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hufford et al., 2012.

claim: Some regions showing evidence of selection during domestication do not contain genes.
source: Intriguingly, some of these regions do not contain genes, and many of the genes identified show differences in expression, pointing to the potentially important role of regulatory variation.
evidence: This is an observation from genomic analysis presented as established knowledge.

claim: Many of the genes identified in regions showing evidence of selection show differences in expression, pointing to the potentially important role of regulatory variation.
source: Intriguingly, some of these regions do not contain genes, and many of the genes identified show differences in expression, pointing to the potentially important role of regulatory variation.
evidence: This is an inference about the importance of regulatory variation based on expression differences.

claim: More than 3000 genes show reduced diversity due to the impact of selection.
source: Overall, more than 3000 genes show reduced diversity due to the impact of selection.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the genomic impact of selection presented as established knowledge.

claim: In spite of strong selection, maize landraces still retain more than 80% of the diversity found in teosinte.
source: In spite of this strong selection, maize landraces still retain more than 80% of the diversity found in teosinte, and it should be possible to identify potentially useful genetic diversity in landraces or teosinte while maintaining the key genetic contributors to improved maize.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about genetic diversity presented as established knowledge.

claim: It should be possible to identify potentially useful genetic diversity in landraces or teosinte while maintaining the key genetic contributors to improved maize.
source: In spite of this strong selection, maize landraces still retain more than 80% of the diversity found in teosinte, and it should be possible to identify potentially useful genetic diversity in landraces or teosinte while maintaining the key genetic contributors to improved maize.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future breeding possibilities indicated by 'should be possible'.

claim: The modern diversity of inbred lines ranges in flowering time from 50 to 120 days and in height from 3 to 15 feet tall.
source: The modern diversity of inbred lines, ranging in their flowering time from 50 to 120 days and in height from 3 to 15 feet tall, derives from maize landraces.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about maize diversity presented as established knowledge.

claim: The modern diversity of inbred lines derives from maize landraces.
source: The modern diversity of inbred lines, ranging in their flowering time from 50 to 120 days and in height from 3 to 15 feet tall, derives from maize landraces.
evidence: This is a statement about the origin of modern maize diversity presented as established knowledge.

claim: Buckler, Holland and McMullen created the nested association mapping (NAM) panel, which consists of 5000 recombinant inbred populations generated by crossing 25 diverse maize lines to the same recurrent parent.
source: Buckler, Holland and McMullen took advantage of this natural diversity to create a widely-used tool, the nested association mapping (NAM) panel, which consists of 5000 recombinant inbred populations (see Glossary) generated by crossing 25 diverse maize lines to the same recurrent parent (McMullen et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McMullen et al., 2009.

claim: The NAM panel is being used to identify the genes responsible for complex traits, such as flowering time, plant architecture, and resistance to pests.
source: This population is being used to identify the genes responsible for complex traits, such as flowering time (Buckler et al., 2009), plant architecture (Brown et al., 2011; Tian et al., 2011), and resistance to pests (Kump et al., 2011; Poland et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Buckler et al., 2009; Brown et al., 2011; Tian et al., 2011; Kump et al., 2011; Poland et al., 2011).

claim: Variation for most traits in maize results from numerous genes that each have a small effect on a trait.
source: It appears that variation for most traits results from numerous genes that each have a small effect on a trait.
evidence: This is a generalization based on genetic studies presented as established knowledge.

claim: Maize differs from self-pollinated species such as rice, sorghum and Arabidopsis, which frequently have fewer loci that produce large effects on traits.
source: Maize differs in this regard from species that are self-pollinated, such as rice, sorghum and Arabidopsis, which frequently have fewer loci that produce large effects on traits (Lin et al., 1995; Salome et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lin et al., 1995; Salome et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2012.

claim: Teosinte, as an out-crossing species, is similar to maize in having variation for most traits result from numerous genes with small effects.
source: Teosinte, as an out-crossing species, is similar to maize in this regard (Weber et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Weber et al., 2008.

claim: Genome wide association studies (GWAS) exploit ancient recombination events that have shuffled and reshuffled genes.
source: Another powerful approach in maize that takes advantage of its diversity and history of outcrossing is that of genome wide association studies (GWAS), which exploits ancient recombination events that have shuffled and reshuffled genes.
evidence: This is a statement about the principle of GWAS presented as established knowledge.

claim: GWAS looks for correlations between variation at individual markers and a trait.
source: GWAS looks for correlations between variation at individual markers and a trait, and has become an important complement to the use of experimental crosses.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology of GWAS presented as established knowledge.

claim: GWAS has become an important complement to the use of experimental crosses.
source: GWAS looks for correlations between variation at individual markers and a trait, and has become an important complement to the use of experimental crosses.
evidence: This is an assessment of the importance of GWAS in maize genetics.

claim: By using detailed genetic and phenotypic information from the NAM line founders and comparing this to genotypic information from their recombinant NAM progeny, we can begin to predict the phenotypic effects produced by the variants of many genes.
source: By using detailed genetic and phenotypic information from the NAM line founders and by comparing this information to genotypic information obtained from their recombinant NAM progeny, we can begin to predict the phenotypic effects produced by the variants of many genes (Wallace et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wallace et al., 2014.

claim: Other collections of maize inbred lines are available for GWAS studies.
source: Other collections of maize inbred lines are also available for GWAS studies (Flint-Garcia et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Flint-Garcia et al., 2005.

claim: A population of 2815 maize lines was genotyped with more than 600,000 single nucleotide polymorphic markers using recently developed, high-throughput sequencing methods.
source: Using recently developed, high-throughput sequencing methods, a population of 2815 maize lines was genotyped with more than 600,000 single nucleotide polymorphic markers (Romay et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Romay et al., 2013.

claim: The density of marker information from 600,000 SNPs worked well for identifying the genetic basis of simple traits using GWAS.
source: This density of marker information worked well for identifying the genetic basis of simple traits using GWAS, but more markers will be needed for analyzing complex traits.
evidence: This is an assessment of the adequacy of marker density for different types of traits.

claim: More markers will be needed for analyzing complex traits using GWAS.
source: This density of marker information worked well for identifying the genetic basis of simple traits using GWAS, but more markers will be needed for analyzing complex traits.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future requirements for GWAS of complex traits.

claim: The eventual goal of these efforts is to link genotypes with phenotypes for use in predictive breeding studies.
source: The eventual goal of these efforts is to link genotypes with phenotypes for use in predictive breeding studies (see Glossary).
evidence: This is a statement about the goal of genetic research in maize.

claim: Predictive breeding will help breeders to create improved crops, by selecting alleles from different inbred maize lines to generate the combination of traits needed in a particular environment.
source: Predictive breeding will help breeders to create improved crops, by selecting alleles from different inbred maize lines to generate the combination of traits needed in a particular environment.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the future application of predictive breeding.

claim: Maize is one of the most important crops worldwide today.
source: Today maize is one of the most important crops worldwide.
evidence: This is a statement about the current importance of maize presented as established knowledge.

claim: Future efforts at incorporating novel alleles into modern germplasm via selective breeding or transgenics will benefit from the history of research in maize and its rich heritage of genetic diversity.
source: Future efforts at incorporating novel alleles into modern germplasm via selective breeding or transgenics, as well as developing predictive breeding models, will benefit from the history of research in maize, as well as its rich heritage of genetic diversity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future breeding efforts.

claim: Developing predictive breeding models will benefit from the history of research in maize and its rich heritage of genetic diversity.
source: Future efforts at incorporating novel alleles into modern germplasm via selective breeding or transgenics, as well as developing predictive breeding models, will benefit from the history of research in maize, as well as its rich heritage of genetic diversity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future breeding efforts.

claim: Maize was domesticated as a model organism, aided in large part by its large chromosomes, ease of pollination and growing agricultural importance.
source: Its domestication eventually led to its adoption as a model organism, aided in large part by its large chromosomes, ease of pollination and growing agricultural importance.
evidence: This is a statement about factors contributing to maize becoming a model organism.

claim: Genome comparisons between varieties of maize, teosinte and other grasses are beginning to identify the genes responsible for the domestication of modern maize.
source: Genome comparisons between varieties of maize, teosinte and other grasses are beginning to identify the genes responsible for the domestication of modern maize and are also providing ideas for the breeding of more hardy varieties.
evidence: This is a statement about ongoing genomic research presented as established knowledge.

claim: Genome comparisons between varieties of maize, teosinte and other grasses are providing ideas for the breeding of more hardy varieties.
source: Genome comparisons between varieties of maize, teosinte and other grasses are beginning to identify the genes responsible for the domestication of modern maize and are also providing ideas for the breeding of more hardy varieties.
evidence: This is a statement about the application of genomic research to breeding.

claim: The word teosinte is derived from 'teocintli'—'teotl' meaning sacred and 'cintli' meaning dried ear of corn—from the indigenous Nahuatl language.
source: The word teosinte is derived from 'teocintli'—'teotl' meaning sacred and 'cintli' meaning dried ear of corn—from the indigenous Nahuatl language.
evidence: This is a statement about etymology presented as established knowledge.

claim: Teosinte refers to all the wild species of Zea that are native to Mexico and Central America.
source: We use the word teosinte to refer to all the wild species of Zea that are native to Mexico and Central America.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about how the term is used in the manuscript.
